introduction-process-serves-the-work.core: Project management is deciding what to work on, in what order, and making sure it gets done. Meetings, boards and charts are tools that should serve that goal, not replace it.

first_principles.problem: Engineers either reject process as bureaucracy or follow rituals mechanically. Both lose sight of shipping the right things.
truths: Every shipped project had some planning.
Process has costs.
Tools are only as good as their use.
derivation: Ask what **problem** a process solves for this team.
Keep the **minimum process** that solves it.

analogy.title: Scaffolding on a building
analogy.story: It's essential while building and pointless if it becomes the building.
analogy.breaks: Scaffolding comes down at the end. Teams need some process permanently, just right-sized.

example.title: A team with too many ceremonies

steps.label: Outcome
steps.detail: Delivery speed rose with fewer meetings.

points: Know what each ritual is for.

check.q: What is project management, at its core?
check.a: Deciding what to work on, in what order, and making sure it gets done.

waterfall-the-predecessor-you-must-under.core: Waterfall runs phases in sequence (requirements → design → build → test → deploy). It suits work where change is expensive and requirements are stable, but fails when learning happens during the project.

first_principles.problem: Software requirements change as users see the product. Waterfall discovers problems only at the end, when they're most expensive to fix.
truths: Waterfall came from construction and manufacturing.
Late feedback is expensive.
Some projects really do have fixed requirements.
derivation: Know **when it fits**: regulated, fixed-scope, hardware-coupled work.
Know **why it fails** for most software: late feedback, big-bang integration.
Borrow its **strengths**: upfront thinking for one-way-door decisions.

analogy.title: Building a bridge
analogy.story: You design fully, then build; changing the design halfway is hugely expensive. That logic was imported into software.
analogy.breaks: Bridges' requirements don't change after opening day. Software's do.

example.title: A year-long project shipped to silence
example.scenario: Users didn't want what was specified a year earlier.

steps.label: Lesson
steps.detail: Feedback came only at the end.

example.outcome: you know why iterative methods emerged.

check.q: Why does waterfall struggle with software?
check.a: Requirements change as users learn, and waterfall only gets feedback at the end.

the-methodologies-agile-scrum-kanban.core: Agile is a philosophy (individuals, working software, collaboration, responding to change). Scrum applies it with fixed sprints and roles; Kanban with continuous flow and work-in-progress limits.

first_principles.problem: Teams 'do Agile' by adopting rituals without the values, or pick Scrum when their work is interrupt-driven (better suited to Kanban).
truths: Short feedback loops reduce risk.
Planned work and interrupt work differ.
Too much WIP slows everything.
derivation: **Scrum**: sprints (1–4 weeks), planning, daily stand-up, review, retro; good for planned feature work.
**Kanban**: visual board, WIP limits, continuous flow; good for ops and support.

analogy.title: A restaurant service
analogy.story: Scrum is a set tasting menu prepared in courses; Kanban is à la carte, orders flowing through with limited burners.
analogy.breaks: Kitchens can see the queue. Software teams need explicit boards to see WIP.

example.title: An SRE team on Scrum
example.scenario: Sprints keep getting blown by incidents.

check.q: When is Kanban a better fit than Scrum?
check.a: For interrupt-driven work like ops or support, where fixed sprints keep breaking.

estimation-story-points-t-shirt-sizing-a.core: Software estimates are unreliable (typically 2–3× low) because work involves discovering unknowns. Use relative sizing, ranges and historical throughput, and estimate only as precisely as the decision needs.

first_principles.problem: Teams spend hours on precise estimates that are wrong anyway, or refuse to estimate and leave stakeholders unable to plan.
truths: Planning fallacy: people underestimate.
Relative comparisons are easier than absolute.
Throughput data predicts better than guesses.
derivation: Match precision to **the decision** it supports.

analogy.title: Estimating a road trip
analogy.story: You know roughly how long similar trips took, but traffic and detours make exact arrival times guesses. A range is honest.
analogy.breaks: Road trips have maps. Software work often creates the map as it goes.

example.title: When will the migration finish?

steps.label: Method
steps.detail: Counting completed items beats hour estimates.

example.outcome: an honest forecast that improves as data accumulates.

check.a: The tendency to underestimate how long tasks will take, identified by Kahneman and Tversky.

roles-product-manager-pm-vs-engineering-.core: The product manager owns what to build and why (user problems, priorities). The engineering manager owns how the team builds it and the people doing it (process, hiring, health). Clear separation avoids conflict.

first_principles.problem: When the PM dictates implementation or the EM sets product priorities alone, decisions get muddled and both roles step on each other.
truths: What and how are different questions.
Both need input from the other.
Unclear ownership causes friction.
derivation: **PM**: user research, roadmap, priorities, success metrics.
**EM**: team health, delivery process, technical quality, hiring.
Decide **together** on trade-offs like scope vs time.

analogy.title: A restaurant's head chef and kitchen manager
analogy.story: The chef decides the menu customers want; the kitchen manager organises staff and stations to deliver it.
analogy.breaks: Restaurant roles are traditional. Tech companies vary, so write down who owns what.

example.title: Tech debt vs features
example.scenario: The EM wants a reliability sprint; the PM has a launch.

steps.label: Outcome
steps.detail: A shared plan instead of a turf war.

example.outcome: clear ownership with shared decisions where they overlap.

check.q: Who typically owns team health and hiring?

ticket-hierarchy-epics-stories-tasks.core: Epics are big initiatives, stories are user-facing slices of value, tasks are concrete technical steps. The hierarchy gives each ticket context and keeps the backlog navigable.

first_principles.problem: A flat list of 1,000 tickets has no context: nobody knows which goal each serves or how close a feature is to done.
truths: Context helps prioritisation.
Value is delivered in user-facing slices.
Work happens in small steps.
derivation: **Story**: a user-visible slice ('As a user I can reset my password').

analogy.title: City, neighbourhoods, buildings
analogy.story: A city map with districts and streets makes any building findable; a flat list of 50,000 addresses doesn't.
analogy.breaks: Cities don't change shape weekly. Backlogs do, so prune them regularly.

example.title: Password reset feature

steps.label: Benefit
steps.detail: Anyone can see how close the epic is to done.

example.outcome: work is organised by the value it delivers.

check.a: A small slice of work that delivers visible value to a user.

meetings-that-matter-running-effective-c.core: Every meeting has a price (6 engineers × 1 hour ≈ $900). Run only meetings with a clear purpose, a decision or output, the right attendees, a time box and recorded follow-ups.

first_principles.problem: Most meetings lack a purpose or a decision, so they cost hundreds of dollars and produce nothing but more meetings.
truths: Meetings cost salaries and focus time.
Unclear goals produce no outcomes.
Async updates often suffice.
derivation: State the **purpose** and **desired output** in the invite.

analogy.title: A taxi meter running
analogy.story: Every minute in a meeting, the meter ticks for everyone in the room. Know your destination before getting in.
analogy.breaks: Taxi fares are visible. Meeting costs are hidden, so make them explicit.

steps.label: Change
steps.detail: Written updates; meeting only for blockers and decisions.

check.q: What should every meeting invite state?
check.a: Its purpose and the decision or output expected.
